extracted.intended_audience: university technology transfer professionals / intellectual property managers and patent counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on international patent prosecution (PCT Chapter I/II, national entry/examination) and comparative novelty standards (U.S., Europe, Japan), plus related copyright considerations for technology transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter II demand and amendment timing
rubrics_metrics.description: If a demand for international preliminary examination (Chapter II) is filed, the ISA-WO will be treated as the initial written opinion by the IPEA; amendments and/or comments should be filed simultaneously with the demand so they can be considered by the IPEA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter II is largely optional but permits dialogue with the international examiner and may be favored if a negative ISA-WO was received in Chapter I. Informal comments submitted during Chapter I will not be considered by the IPEA; Article 19 amendments may be considered upon request by an applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPRP (Ch. II) contents and public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chapter II international preliminary report on patentability (IPRP (Ch. II)) provides an opinion on novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability and points out objections to claim form or clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IPRP (Ch. II) is made available to each elected patent office and becomes publicly available via the IB after 30 months from the earliest priority date; prosecution history may become public earlier through elected offices (e.g., EPO permits public file inspection). If confidentiality of prosecution is critical, consider implications of elected-office disclosure rules and selecting an IPEA (e.g., USPTO) accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: National conversion deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Chapter II process, an applicant must decide at thirty (or in some cases thirty-one) months from the earliest priority date whether to convert the international application into national applications in elected member countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decision point is the deadline to enter national/regional phases and begin national prosecution in desired jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing national prosecution and counsel coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Once national conversion/entry occurs, the application enters the national examination process in each country or region where protection is sought; this process is typically the most complex and expensive part of obtaining foreign patent rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual property managers should work closely with foreign patent counsel to manage prosecution of each foreign case and ensure prosecution strategies across jurisdictions are consistent. Initially rely on foreign counsel’s advice; with experience, take a more proactive role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute vs. relative novelty (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions apply an absolute novelty standard (invention is not novel if it was made available to the public anywhere prior to filing), while others apply a relative novelty standard (limitations on nature, place, or time of prior disclosures that will be destructive of novelty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute novelty broadly treats any public disclosure anywhere as anticipating; relative novelty (e.g., historic U.S. approach) may limit what counts as prior art (e.g., prior use only invalidating if it occurred in the U.S.). Always check jurisdiction-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: European novelty standard and exceptions (EPC Article 54 & 55)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EPC Article 54, the state of the art comprises everything made available to the public by written/oral description, use, or any other way before the filing date; information disclosed under confidentiality is not part of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single sales anywhere can destroy novelty, and prior unprinted specifications opened to public inspection are destructive. EPC Article 55 provides limited exceptions: disclosures within six months before filing may not be destructive if made by the applicant at qualifying exhibitions or made by a third party against the applicant’s will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japanese novelty standard and exceptions (JPL Sections 29 & 30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 29 of the JPL treats an invention as novel if it was not publicly known, publicly worked, or described in a distributed publication/electronic means in Japan or elsewhere prior to filing; Section 30 provides exceptions for disclosures no more than six months prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JPL exceptions include experimental use by the inventor, inventor publications/disclosures, presentations at designated scientific organizations, acts by third parties against the applicant’s will, and presentations at officially recognized exhibitions. The Japanese six-month grace period is broader than the European one, expressly including experimental uses and inventor publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. novelty standard and statutory bars/exceptions (35 U.S.C. §102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. law, a person is not entitled to a patent if the invention was known or used by others in this country or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country prior to the invention, or if the invention was patented/printed/public use/on sale in this country more than one year prior to the U.S. application (35 U.S.C. §102(a) and §102(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critical date for U.S. novelty inquiries is typically the date of invention (with limited exceptions where filing date controls). §102(b) introduces a one-year statutory bar that can expand what counts as anticipatory prior art. Prior uses may be limited by location (e.g., prior use invalidating only if in the U.S.); however, all sales are destructive of novelty regardless of secrecy. There are exceptions for secret knowledge/uses and certain public experimental uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider jurisdiction-specific novelty consequences when strategizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in novelty standards among jurisdictions (U.S., Europe, Japan) can preclude obtaining patent protection in particular nations based on the same disclosure history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning filings and public disclosures, evaluate where and when disclosures/sales/uses occur relative to the filing/priority date and applicable national standards; consult foreign counsel for jurisdiction-specific advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPRP/ISA-WO as substantive inputs to national prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: The ISA Written Opinion and IPRP (Ch. II) provide opinions on novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability that elected patent offices will see and may use during national prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A negative ISA-WO may prompt use of Chapter II to engage with the examiner; consider timing and content of amendments/comments to influence eventual national examination outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright subject matter and ownership (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects original works of authorship fixed in a tangible medium; generally the author or the author’s employer is the copyright owner; registration is not required for protection but provides enhanced rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyright does not extend to scientific or historic facts; separate elements (software, music, images) in multimedia works may have separate owners. Consider trade secret, contract, or patent protection where copyright is inapplicable (e.g., software may be protected by copyright, trade secret, or patent law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of exclusive copyright rights and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright grants exclusive rights to reproduce the work, prepare derivative works, distribute copies, perform publicly, and display publicly; certain visual artists also have attribution/integrity rights. Copyright does not protect ideas, procedures, processes, systems, methods of operation, concepts, principles, or discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When licensing or exploiting works, be mindful which exclusive rights are being transferred; understand that factual/material components may not be subject to copyright protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative works: definition, ownership, and infringement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivative work is based upon one or more preexisting works and includes editorial revisions, annotations, elaborations, or other modifications that as a whole represent original authorship; the derivative must reflect at least a minimal degree of creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermediate copies in software development or database creation can be infringing derivative works. The original author retains copyright in preexisting material; a second author owns copyright in new material contributed if creation was authorized. Licensees are not ordinarily authorized to prepare derivative works. Proving infringement may require showing substantial similarity; proof that the derivative is independently copyrightable is not always required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compilations and database copyright protection
rubrics_metrics.description: A compilation is material selected, coordinated, or arranged to constitute an original work of authorship; protection requires (1) collection/assembly of preexisting data, (2) selection/coordination/arrangement, and (3) resulting originality by virtue of that selection/arrangement. Factual data receives thin protection; purely factual material is unprotected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mechanical or routine selection lacks sufficient creativity. Compilations of less than four selections are presumed to lack authorship. To enhance protection of databases, include creative material/organization and descriptive or normative terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Database protection legislative landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to limited copyright protection for databases, database owners often rely on trade secret law, access-limiting contracts, or seek sui generis database protection (e.g., EU Database Directive provides 15-year protection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. firms historically could not rely on the EU directive without reciprocal protection; proposals for U.S. database protection have not been enacted. Consider technical, contractual, and trade-secret measures in addition to copyright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic republication rights and contract drafting (Tasini principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Republishing freelance works electronically (e.g., on databases, CD-ROMs, websites) may not be authorized by prior publication rights; electronic republication can create a new collective work rather than a permissible revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts/licensing of third-party content should include explicit provisions addressing electronic republication rights. Authors and publishers should renegotiate to clarify electronic rights; licensors should expressly secure the intended electronic rights to avoid infringement claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work-for-hire presumption for employee-created works
rubrics_metrics.description: If material is created by an employee within the scope of employment, the Copyright Act presumes the employer owns the copyright as a work made for hire (17 U.S.C. §201(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To rebut the presumption, a written agreement signed by both parties may be necessary. Courts apply common-law agency tests (see Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid) considering multiple factors (control over manner/means, skill required, tools provided, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specially commissioned works: categories and written agreement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-employee commissioned works can be treated as works for hire only if (1) the work falls into a statutory category (e.g., contribution to a collective work, audiovisual work, translation, compilation, instructional text, test material, atlas) and (2) parties expressly agree in a written instrument signed by them that the work is a work made for hire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The parties must agree prior to creation that the work will be a work for hire (though the writing memorializing the agreement may be executed after creation). Software rarely qualifies as a specially commissioned category, so independent-contractor-created software usually remains owned by the contractor absent assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining employee status and scope of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee status for copyright purposes is determined by common-law agency factors (control, skill, tools, location, duration, assignment rights, discretion, method of payment, benefits, tax treatment, etc.). Conduct is within the scope of employment if it is of the kind the employee was hired to perform, occurs substantially within authorized work hours, and is actuated at least in part to serve the employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single factor is dispositive. Case law indicates that even off-hours work may be within the scope if it serves the employer (e.g., software developed by an employee to improve employer processes may be within scope). Employers should secure written assignments where ownership is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and termination of copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright duration: life of the author plus 70 years for single authors; life of last surviving author plus 70 years for joint works; works for hire: 95 years from publication or 120 years from creation (whichever expires first). Authors (or heirs) have a statutory right to terminate transfers/licenses approximately 35 years from publication or 40 years from grant, except for works made for hire which are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Termination rights are nonassignable and cannot be waived in advance. Parties dealing with long-term transfers should account for potential statutory termination and exclusion of works for hire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to universities and scholarly-works practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities must generally obtain a written signed agreement to rebut the presumption that materials created in the course of employment are works for hire; traditionally, universities have not claimed copyrights in scholarly works (faculty articles) and courts have recognized academic tradition of faculty ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: University policies should be explicit and signed to affect ownership. In practice, universities often avoid claiming scholarly works, though disputes have arisen; analyze policy language and statutory rules to determine ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint authorship criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint work is prepared by two or more authors with the intention that their contributions be merged into inseparable or interdependent parts of a unitary whole. A contribution produces co-ownership only if it represents original expression that could stand on its own as the subject matter of copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent to merge contributions and sufficiency of each contribution (original expression) are key. Use clear agreements to define rights among collaborators.
